column1: # Every body in this directory, the diff it is read against, and the verdict
# `pr-body.sh` has to reach. Each one was rendered through GitHub's own
# markdown API first, so the expectation is what a reader actually sees and
# One image on an allowed host is enough, even beside one that is not:
# the rule is that the body carries durable evidence, not that nothing else
# appears near it. Pinned here so it stays a decision rather than an accident.
# A `<!--` that opens mid-sentence and is never closed is literal text on the
# page — the reader sees it. Eating the description on account of it is the
# sibling of the code-fence bug, and refusing an honest body is worse than
# The control for the two above, and the one that matters most: the dark-mode
# idiom written honestly, both URLs on an allowed host. Refusing this would
# punish people for following GitHub's own documentation.
# A decoy attribute placed before the real one. A bare \b catches the `src`
# inside `data-src`, and the lazy match ahead of it took the first thing it
# found, so the decoy was what got read. The lookbehind is what closed it.
# `srcset` on an `` was never a way in and no code was added for it: `src`
# there is followed by `set` rather than `=`, so the matcher walks past it to
# the real one, and GitHub strips `srcset` from an `` anyway. Kept because
# a direction nobody is defending is the one that quietly stops being true.
# The live version of this is `<source srcset>`, two blocks down.
# A `` shows its first matching `` and keeps the `` only
# as a fallback, and GitHub preserves `<source srcset>` without proxying it. So
# a fork-hosted `` is what a reader sees and the allowlisted ``
# behind it never loads. The `media` spelling is GitHub's own dark-mode idiom,
# which shows the fork to every reviewer in dark mode and to nobody else.
# The same hiding trick, reached through an inline code span that appears to
# wrap the comment opener. It does not: the renderer settles blocks before it
# looks at anything inline, so this renders as one line of prose.
